LENDING.flavor: Where the bank branches thin out, the storefront lenders fill in.

HOUSING.flavor: Historic homes, empty lots, and families who never left.

LABOR.flavor: GM's Moraine plant closed in 2008 and NCR moved its headquarters out in 2009. The good jobs left; the fine print didn't.

HEALTH.flavor: Good Samaritan Hospital in northwest Dayton closed in 2018. Care got farther away; the bills didn't.

EDUCATION.flavor: Paul Laurence Dunbar High School, Sinclair downtown, Wilberforce and Central State down the road.

LENDING.front: Quick Cash: $375 today. One flat fee — $56.25.
LENDING.red: That fee is a 391% APR. The fee is the product, not a favor.
LENDING.amber: Due in full in 14 days. Can't pay? You 'reroll' and owe $56.25 again.
LENDING.blue: The storefront and the debt buyer that hounds you later share one owner.
LENDING.basis: a $56.25 fee paid 8 times, like the typical payday borrower

LENDING.front: Title Loan: borrow $1,000 on your car title, keep driving.
LENDING.red: ~300% APR, and the loan is a fraction of the car's real value.
LENDING.amber: One missed payment = repossession, often with no grace period.
LENDING.blue: The lender holds a stake in the repo lot that resells your car.
LENDING.basis: 25% a month on $1,000, for 5 months

LENDING.front: Pawn: cash now for your item, buy it back anytime.
LENDING.red: Effective APR 120–240%; most items are never redeemed.
LENDING.amber: The redemption window is short — miss it and it's sold.
LENDING.blue: Resale profit flows to the same chain that wrote the loan.
LENDING.basis: 20% a month on a $250 pawn, for 3 months

LENDING.front: Buy Now, Pay Later: 4 easy payments, 0% interest!
LENDING.red: Late fees pile on, and it stacks across apps till you lose track.
LENDING.amber: Autopay hits whether the money's there or not → overdraft.
LENDING.blue: The BNPL firm sells your payment data and routes late fees up.
LENDING.basis: seven $10 late fees across overdue plans

LENDING.front: Overdraft Protection: we'll cover your card if you're short.
LENDING.red: Up to ~$35 per swipe — a $4 coffee can cost ~$39 (many banks now $0–$15).
LENDING.amber: Charges reordered largest-first to trigger the most fees.
LENDING.blue: Overdraft fees are a top profit line for the bank behind it.
LENDING.basis: five $35 overdraft fees in a month

LENDING.front: Cash Advance App: get $100 early. No interest — just tip!
LENDING.red: A $14 'tip' + fee on $100 for a week ≈ 300%+ APR.
LENDING.amber: Auto-debits on payday; bad timing sets off an overdraft cascade.
LENDING.blue: The 'tip' dodges lending law; the app sells your bank data.
LENDING.basis: a $14 tip-and-fee, eight times a year

LENDING.front: Refund Advance: your tax refund NOW, don't wait weeks.
LENDING.red: Fees + interest eat a refund you'd get free in a few days.
LENDING.amber: Due when the IRS pays — any delay becomes your problem.
LENDING.blue: The preparer, the bank, and the loan are one packaged product.
LENDING.basis: advance and filing fees on a refund that was coming anyway

LENDING.front: Online Installment Loan: need $2,000? Easy approval.
LENDING.red: 100%+ APR by renting an out-of-state bank to dodge your state's cap.
LENDING.amber: Balloon structure — early payments barely touch the principal.
LENDING.blue: A fintech fronts it; a far-off bank lends its charter for a cut.
LENDING.basis: about 100% a year on $2,000 over 18 months

LENDING.front: Credit Builder: build your credit — guaranteed approval!
LENDING.red: You pay fees for a 'loan' you can't touch; it may not even report.
LENDING.amber: Cancel late and you eat months of fees for nothing.
LENDING.blue: The fees are the business; your 'credit building' is the bait.
LENDING.basis: $15 a month in fees for a year, on a loan you can't touch

LENDING.front: Debt Consolidation: one low monthly payment, be debt-free!
LENDING.red: Lower payment = longer term = more interest paid in total.
LENDING.amber: Stop paying creditors as told and your credit craters first.
LENDING.blue: The 'nonprofit' is funded by fees from the lenders it deals with.
LENDING.basis: a $10,000 balance stretched from 3 years to 5, at 17%

LENDING.front: Drive It Home Today — financing approved!
LENDING.red: Days later: 'financing fell through,' re-signed at a worse rate.
LENDING.amber: They hold your trade-in and down payment hostage to force the redo.
LENDING.blue: The dealer and the finance arm split the markup on your rate.
LENDING.basis: re-signed at a worse rate after the 'financing fell through'

LENDING.front: Check Cashing: cash your check instantly, no bank needed.
LENDING.red: 1–5% per check — hundreds a year to reach your own money.
LENDING.amber: Every payday, every time. It never stops.
LENDING.blue: The chain also sells the payday loans you'll 'need' next.
LENDING.basis: 2% of a $20,000-a-year paycheck, for a year

LENDING.front: Credit-union personal loan: fixed low rate.
LENDING.red: A fair APR — the rate is the whole story, no hidden second number.
LENDING.amber: No prepayment penalty; pay it early and save.
LENDING.blue: Member-owned nonprofit; the profit returns to members like you.
LENDING.basis: what a fair rate saves over a high-cost loan

LENDING.front: Layaway: pay it off first, then take it home.
LENDING.red: No interest and no debt — you only pay the sticker price.
LENDING.amber: Miss payments and you just get your money back, minus a small fee.
LENDING.blue: Old-school model with nobody profiting off your debt.
LENDING.basis: no interest and no fees

LENDING.front: Free tax prep (VITA) + your refund by direct deposit.
LENDING.red: $0 to file, and the full refund is yours — no advance fee.
LENDING.amber: E-file with direct deposit and it usually lands in about 3 weeks.
LENDING.blue: An IRS-backed volunteer program; nobody earns a cut of your refund.
LENDING.basis: a typical tax-prep fee, kept

HOUSING.front: Rent-to-Own: $25/week and the couch is yours!
HOUSING.red: Total paid = 2–4x the retail price.
HOUSING.amber: Miss one week late in the term and they take it — you keep nothing.
HOUSING.blue: The store and the lease company are one holding company.
HOUSING.basis: $25 a week for a year, for a couch that sells for about $400

HOUSING.front: No-Credit-Check Lease: bad credit? Move in today.
HOUSING.red: Huge deposit + junk fees; rent set above market for 'risk'.
HOUSING.amber: A 60-day move-out notice is buried inside — miss it, it auto-renews.
HOUSING.blue: The 'management co.' is a shell of the same landlord group.
HOUSING.basis: a big deposit and a 'risk' markup in the first year

HOUSING.front: Own Your Home — no bank, no mortgage! (Contract-for-Deed)
HOUSING.red: You build no equity; miss a payment late and lose it all.
HOUSING.amber: One default — even near the end — forfeits everything you paid.
HOUSING.blue: The seller reclaims and resells the same house again and again.
HOUSING.basis: years of payments on a house you never own, gone with one late payment

HOUSING.front: Rent is only $950!
HOUSING.red: 'Technology fee,' 'convenience fee,' 'valet trash' add $100+/mo.
HOUSING.amber: Fees climb at renewal while the base rent stays 'the same'.
HOUSING.blue: A third-party fee processor splits the take with the landlord.
HOUSING.basis: $100 a month in junk fees, for a year

HOUSING.front: Just first month + deposit to move in.
HOUSING.red: Move-out charges get invented to keep your whole deposit.
HOUSING.amber: The dispute window is tight — miss it and it's gone.
HOUSING.blue: A 'turnover' vendor profits from every withheld deposit.
HOUSING.basis: a deposit kept for invented move-out charges

HOUSING.front: $50 to apply — refundable if you're not approved!
HOUSING.red: Rarely refunded; they collect from dozens for one open unit.
HOUSING.amber: Your decision stays 'pending' past the refund window.
HOUSING.blue: The screening company and the landlord share the fee pool.
HOUSING.basis: five $50 applications

HOUSING.front: Renters insurance included for your protection.
HOUSING.red: A marked-up policy that mostly protects the landlord, not you.
HOUSING.amber: Auto-added monthly; opting out is hidden and time-boxed.
HOUSING.blue: The landlord earns a commission on every policy.
HOUSING.basis: a $10-a-month markup on the policy, for a year

HOUSING.front: Welcome! Great intro rent.
HOUSING.red: Renewal jumps 15–30%; moving costs trap you into paying it.
HOUSING.amber: Your notice to leave is due before you even learn the new rate.
HOUSING.blue: Rent-setting software coordinates the hike across the whole area.
HOUSING.basis: a 20% renewal hike on $1,000 rent, for a year

HOUSING.front: Low payment to get you in the door! (ARM mortgage)
HOUSING.red: The teaser rate resets far higher — your payment can double.
HOUSING.amber: The reset date was set on day one; the clock always ran.
HOUSING.blue: The loan is sold upstream; the servicer profits when you struggle.
HOUSING.basis: a $500 payment that resets to $1,000, for a year

HOUSING.front: All utilities included — simple!
HOUSING.red: A flat 'utility' charge set far above your real usage.
HOUSING.amber: The rate adjusts up yearly with no itemized proof.
HOUSING.blue: A submetering vendor splits the overcharge with ownership.
HOUSING.basis: $50 a month above real usage, for a year

HOUSING.front: Standard lease, just sign here.
HOUSING.red: Waives your notice and auto-adds 'attorney fees' on any late rent.
HOUSING.amber: Late by a day → filing starts and fees attach immediately.
HOUSING.blue: A high-volume eviction law firm is paid per filing by the group.
HOUSING.basis: attorney fees added to one late rent

HOUSING.front: First month FREE!
HOUSING.red: Leave early and you repay the 'free' month plus a penalty.
HOUSING.amber: The clawback triggers on any break before month 13.
HOUSING.blue: Concessions are booked as debt you owe the property fund.
HOUSING.basis: the 'free' month paid back, plus a penalty

HOUSING.front: A fair lease: normal deposit, clear terms.
HOUSING.red: Rent is the rent — deposit is refundable, fees are spelled out.
HOUSING.amber: Standard notice period, plainly stated. No buried clause.
HOUSING.blue: A small local landlord, not a shell of a national fund.
HOUSING.basis: a deposit you actually get back

HOUSING.front: Housing voucher (Section 8): inspected unit, capped rent.
HOUSING.red: Your share of rent is capped to your income — the real cost is low.
HOUSING.amber: Annual recertification, clearly scheduled.
HOUSING.blue: A public program built to keep you housed, not to extract.
HOUSING.basis: a year of rent above your capped share

HOUSING.front: Community land trust home: buy at a price you can afford.
HOUSING.red: A real mortgage you can carry; you build equity as you pay.
HOUSING.amber: Resale is capped, and that's spelled out on day one.
HOUSING.blue: The trust holds the land so the next family can afford it too.
HOUSING.basis: equity built in the first years

LABOR.front: Sign here to start Monday.
LABOR.red: You waive your right to sue or join a class action.
LABOR.amber: The 30-day opt-out is buried on page 9 — the clock starts now.
LABOR.blue: The arbitration firm is chosen and paid by the employer.
LABOR.basis: a wage claim you signed away

LABOR.front: Standard new-hire paperwork. (Non-compete)
LABOR.red: Can block you from your whole field for a year+ (enforceability varies by state).
LABOR.amber: Signed at hire; enforced exactly when you try to leave.
LABOR.blue: Used to hold wages down across an entire local industry.
LABOR.basis: a year kept out of better pay in your field

LABOR.front: You're an independent contractor — be your own boss!
LABOR.red: No overtime, no benefits; you pay both halves of payroll tax.
LABOR.amber: Back-pay and benefit claims expire if you don't file in time.
LABOR.blue: The staffing agency pockets what your protections would've cost.
LABOR.basis: the employer's half of payroll tax, overtime and benefits, on $35,000

LABOR.front: Tips pooled and shared fairly, trust us.
LABOR.red: Managers skim the pool; off-clock work goes unpaid.
LABOR.amber: Wage claims have a filing deadline, and proof fades fast.
LABOR.blue: Skimmed wages become the owner's margin.
LABOR.basis: skimmed tips and unpaid off-clock work, over a year

LABOR.front: Free training to start your career!
LABOR.red: Quit within 2 years and owe thousands for that 'training'.
LABOR.amber: The debt clock starts day one and follows you out the door.
LABOR.blue: The 'debt' is sold to a collector the moment you leave.
LABOR.basis: paying back 'free' training after quitting early

LABOR.front: Come do a working interview!
LABOR.red: Hours of real labor with no pay — and often no job after.
LABOR.amber: 'We'll decide later' — payday never comes.
LABOR.blue: Serial trial shifts quietly staff the floor for free.
LABOR.basis: an unpaid 8-hour day at $15 an hour

LABOR.front: Flexible hours — we'll text you!
LABOR.red: You hold the day open, get called off, and earn nothing.
LABOR.amber: Hours cut just below the benefits threshold on purpose.
LABOR.blue: Scheduling software optimizes you to part-time, no benefits.
LABOR.basis: called-off shifts over a year

LABOR.front: Get paid on a convenient card!
LABOR.red: Fees to check your balance, to withdraw, even to stay active.
LABOR.amber: Inactivity fees drain it if you don't cash out fast.
LABOR.blue: The card issuer and employer split the fee revenue.
LABOR.basis: card fees over a year

LABOR.front: Shop at our store with your staff discount!
LABOR.red: Wages steered back to the employer at marked-up prices.
LABOR.amber: Advances against pay keep you one cycle behind, always.
LABOR.blue: The modern company town — you owe your soul to the store.
LABOR.basis: wages spent back at marked-up prices

LABOR.front: Set your own schedule, earn per job!
LABOR.red: Pay per task drops as you come to rely on it; costs are all yours.
LABOR.amber: Incentives expire; the 'bonus' always moves out of reach.
LABOR.blue: The platform tunes your pay to the lowest you'll still accept.
LABOR.basis: car costs and falling per-job pay, over a year

LABOR.front: Congrats, you're salaried now — a manager!
LABOR.red: A 'manager' title used to dodge overtime on 60-hour weeks.
LABOR.amber: Your duties never match the title; claims expire quietly.
LABOR.blue: Your unpaid overtime is pure profit upstream.
LABOR.basis: unpaid overtime on 60-hour weeks, for a year

LABOR.front: Quick team meeting after your shift.
LABOR.red: Off-clock captive meetings, with anti-organizing pressure.
LABOR.amber: Attendance is tracked; refusing is quietly punished.
LABOR.blue: Union-avoidance consultants are paid to keep you quiet.
LABOR.basis: off-clock meetings over a year

LABOR.front: A real W-2 job: overtime, benefits, clear pay.
LABOR.red: You get overtime, the employer pays its share of taxes, benefits included.
LABOR.amber: Pay schedule and raises are written and predictable.
LABOR.blue: Classified correctly — your protections are intact.
LABOR.basis: overtime, benefits and the employer's tax share

LABOR.front: Union apprenticeship: paid training, raises you keep.
LABOR.red: You're paid to learn, and the skill and raises are yours for good.
LABOR.amber: A clear schedule of raises as you hit milestones.
LABOR.blue: Collective bargaining puts the leverage on your side.
LABOR.basis: paid training and the raises that come with it

LABOR.front: File a wage claim with the state labor office.
LABOR.red: Free to file — and it's illegal for the boss to retaliate.
LABOR.amber: The deadline is long, but file soon while the records are fresh.
LABOR.blue: The public enforcer works for you, not the employer.
LABOR.basis: back wages recovered

HEALTH.front: In-network hospital — you're covered.
HEALTH.red: An out-of-network doctor inside it bills you the gap.
HEALTH.amber: Since 2022 the No Surprises Act bans this for ER/emergency care — dispute it.
HEALTH.blue: Staffing firms place out-of-network docs in in-network ERs on purpose.

HEALTH.front: Amount due: $8,400. FINAL.
HEALTH.red: It's an opening offer — cash and charity rates are far lower.
HEALTH.amber: Negotiate before it hits collections or the number hardens.
HEALTH.blue: Hospital, biller, and collector are one revenue chain.
HEALTH.basis: paying the opening price instead of the charity or cash rate

HEALTH.front: Medical card: 0% interest if paid in 12 months!
HEALTH.red: Deferred interest — miss the date and they backdate ALL of it.
HEALTH.amber: The 0% clock ends quietly on a date you'll forget.
HEALTH.blue: The clinic earns a cut for every patient it signs up.
HEALTH.basis: deferred interest backdated on a $2,500 bill

HEALTH.front: Just a routine clinic visit.
HEALTH.red: A separate 'facility fee' for the room — often more than the visit.
HEALTH.amber: It shows up weeks later as a second, surprise bill.
HEALTH.blue: Hospitals buy up clinics just to attach facility fees.
HEALTH.basis: a facility fee on top of the visit

HEALTH.front: Please pay your balance today.
HEALTH.red: You likely qualify for charity care they never mentioned.
HEALTH.amber: Eligibility windows close while they push you to pay.
HEALTH.blue: Nonprofits owe charity care but profit by collecting instead.
HEALTH.basis: paying a bill charity care would have cut

HEALTH.front: Health coverage for just $99/mo! (Short-term plan)
HEALTH.red: Denies pre-existing conditions; caps leave you exposed.
HEALTH.amber: Claims denied after care, and appeal windows are short.
HEALTH.blue: The broker earns a fat commission on junk plans.
HEALTH.basis: a denied claim after a year of premiums

HEALTH.front: We can set up a payment plan.
HEALTH.red: The plan reports to credit and can lead to liens or garnishment.
HEALTH.amber: Statute-of-limitations tricks restart the debt clock.
HEALTH.blue: The debt is sold for pennies; the collector profits on the spread.
HEALTH.basis: a payment plan sent to collections

HEALTH.front: Your copay is $60.
HEALTH.red: The cash price can be lower than your insured copay.
HEALTH.amber: 'Gag clauses' once barred pharmacists from telling you.
HEALTH.blue: Pharmacy middlemen pocket the spread between list and real price.
HEALTH.basis: a copay above the cash price

HEALTH.front: We'll get you to the hospital. (Ambulance)
HEALTH.red: Ground ambulances are often out-of-network — and still exempt from the No Surprises Act.
HEALTH.amber: The bill arrives later; you had no way to choose in the moment.
HEALTH.blue: Private-equity-owned ambulance firms balance-bill on purpose.

HEALTH.front: Here's your total, pay at the desk.
HEALTH.red: Errors and duplicate charges hide in the itemization you didn't see.
HEALTH.amber: Request the itemized bill fast — before it's marked 'final'.
HEALTH.blue: Upcoding inflates the bill; the chain keeps the overcharge.

HEALTH.front: Get the dental work done now — finance it!
HEALTH.red: In-office financing at high deferred interest.
HEALTH.amber: The promo ends mid-treatment and the rate jumps.
HEALTH.blue: The provider is paid upfront; you're left owing the lender.

HEALTH.front: We'll airlift you — don't worry about the cost.
HEALTH.red: Air-ambulance bills run $30k–$50k — but the No Surprises Act (2022) now shields most of it.
HEALTH.amber: You still can't consent to the price mid-emergency, so know your protection.
HEALTH.blue: PE-owned air fleets long relied on balance billing as the business model.
HEALTH.basis: what's left after the No Surprises Act covers most of it

HEALTH.front: Charity-care application at a nonprofit hospital.
HEALTH.red: You likely qualify — the real cost could be $0 to a small fraction.
HEALTH.amber: Apply within the window and the balance can be wiped.
HEALTH.blue: Nonprofit hospitals are required to offer this; it's your right.
HEALTH.basis: a hospital bill cut by charity care

HEALTH.front: Join Gem City Market: a grocery the neighborhood owns.
HEALTH.red: Membership is a share in the store, not a subscription. Fresh food close to home.
HEALTH.amber: No teaser price, no auto-renew trap. The rules are the co-op's bylaws, in the open.
HEALTH.blue: Member-owned: the store answers to the people it feeds.
HEALTH.basis: fresh food close to home, and a share in the store

HEALTH.front: Community clinic, sliding-scale fee.
HEALTH.red: The price is matched to your income — no surprise markup.
HEALTH.amber: Set your fee up front; no bill ambush later.
HEALTH.blue: Federally supported care designed to reach everyone.
HEALTH.basis: a visit priced to your income

HEALTH.front: Marketplace plan with an income-based subsidy.
HEALTH.red: Covers pre-existing conditions; the subsidy cuts the premium.
HEALTH.amber: Sign up in open enrollment, or within 60 days of a life change.
HEALTH.blue: A public program with real rules; the plan can't deny you for being sick.

EDUCATION.front: Enroll now — job placement guaranteed!
EDUCATION.red: Low grad rates; 'placement' counts any job, not the career.
EDUCATION.amber: The enrollment deadline pushes you past the refund date.
EDUCATION.blue: The school and the loan servicer are one owner.
EDUCATION.basis: for-profit tuition for a credential that doesn't lead to the career

EDUCATION.front: Approved! A private loan to cover your whole tuition.
EDUCATION.red: Variable rate, fewer protections than federal — take federal first.
EDUCATION.amber: The rate resets on a schedule you don't control.
EDUCATION.blue: The servicer profits the longer you stay in debt.
EDUCATION.basis: extra interest over a federal loan

EDUCATION.front: Pay $0 now — just a % of your future income! (ISA)
EDUCATION.red: Can cost far more than a normal loan if you actually succeed.
EDUCATION.amber: The percentage and term lock in before you know your salary.
EDUCATION.blue: Investors bought a slice of your future paycheck.
EDUCATION.basis: income-share payments above a normal loan, if you do well

EDUCATION.front: Just have a family member cosign.
EDUCATION.red: The cosigner is fully liable; default wrecks their credit too.
EDUCATION.amber: The 'release' option has conditions almost no one ever meets.
EDUCATION.blue: Binding family debt is a feature, not a bug, for the lender.
EDUCATION.basis: a cosigned loan that defaults

EDUCATION.front: Can't pay? Just defer — no worries!
EDUCATION.red: Unpaid interest is added to principal; the debt grows while you wait.
EDUCATION.amber: Capitalization hits on a date buried in the terms.
EDUCATION.blue: A bigger balance means more servicer profit.
EDUCATION.basis: interest added to the loan while it was deferred

EDUCATION.front: 6 weeks to a high-paying certification!
EDUCATION.red: A credential employers don't recognize, with sky-high fees.
EDUCATION.amber: No refund once the first module 'starts'.
EDUCATION.blue: The 'accreditor' is paid by the schools it blesses.
EDUCATION.basis: fees for a credential employers don't recognize

EDUCATION.front: Start here, transfer anywhere later!
EDUCATION.red: The credits don't transfer; you pay to retake them.
EDUCATION.amber: You find out only after you've enrolled and paid.
EDUCATION.blue: Non-transferable credits lock you into one paying school.
EDUCATION.basis: paying to retake credits that didn't transfer

EDUCATION.front: Tuition is all-inclusive!
EDUCATION.red: Mandatory 'lab,' 'tech,' and book fees stack up fast.
EDUCATION.amber: Fees are billed per term and rise each year.
EDUCATION.blue: A captive bookstore/vendor shares in the markup.
EDUCATION.basis: lab, tech and book fees on 'all-inclusive' tuition

EDUCATION.front: A counselor will help you apply today!
EDUCATION.red: 'Counselors' are commissioned salespeople hitting enrollment quotas.
EDUCATION.amber: High pressure: 'enroll today or lose your spot.'
EDUCATION.blue: Recruiters are paid per signed enrollment, not per graduate.
EDUCATION.basis: a commissioned sale into the wrong program

EDUCATION.front: We'll erase your student loans — for a fee!
EDUCATION.red: Charges you for free federal programs; can forfeit protections.
EDUCATION.amber: Pay upfront, then 'processing' drags past your real options.
EDUCATION.blue: A fee-mill resells your info to the next scam in line.
EDUCATION.basis: fees for free federal programs

EDUCATION.front: No cost until you're hired at $70k+! (Bootcamp ISA)
EDUCATION.red: Broad definitions of 'hired' trigger payments even on low pay.
EDUCATION.amber: The clock and salary floor are written to favor the school.
EDUCATION.blue: Financiers bundle and securitize cohorts of students like bonds.
EDUCATION.basis: income-share payments on low pay

EDUCATION.front: Keep your license current — easy subscription.
EDUCATION.red: Auto-renews yearly at a higher rate for credits you're required to have.
EDUCATION.amber: The cancel window is tiny and lands right before renewal.
EDUCATION.blue: A captive provider holds a monopoly on the required credits.
EDUCATION.basis: auto-renewal price hikes

EDUCATION.front: Federal student aid (FAFSA): fixed rate, protections.
EDUCATION.red: Fixed rate, income-driven repayment, forgiveness options — take this first.
EDUCATION.amber: Clear, federal timelines; deferment won't quietly capitalize the same way.
EDUCATION.blue: Public aid built for you, not an investor's return.
EDUCATION.basis: federal protections over a private loan

EDUCATION.front: Public library / free certification program.
EDUCATION.red: Real, recognized skills for $0 — the cost is just your time.
EDUCATION.amber: Go at your own pace; no refund deadline to beat.
EDUCATION.blue: A public good with nobody profiting off your enrollment.
EDUCATION.basis: a free certification

EDUCATION.front: Community college with a guaranteed-transfer agreement.
EDUCATION.red: Low tuition, and the credits are guaranteed to count at the state school.
EDUCATION.amber: Follow the transfer map from semester one.
EDUCATION.blue: A public partnership — the schools are built to pass you along, not trap you.
EDUCATION.basis: two years at community-college prices that transfer

roles.Translator: Teaches for free (no Trust cost). Still has to read a district to teach it. The bridge — spreads the Read fastest.
roles.Student: Gains DOUBLE Read when taught. The hungry one.
roles.Elder: Starts with Read 1 everywhere; once per game, 'Teach the History' wakes a whole district instantly.
roles.Veteran: Shields the block from two Machine hits per game. Came home to protect it.
roles.Organizer: A successful NEGOTIATE drops Squeeze by 2, not 1 (collective action). Rallies the block.

patterns.name: REDLINING
patterns.lesson: Credit and housing denied by geography — your address decides what money costs you.

patterns.name: THE MEDICAL-DEBT SPIRAL
patterns.lesson: One illness becomes a debt becomes ruined credit. A leading cause of bankruptcy in America.

patterns.name: THE DEBT DIPLOMA
patterns.lesson: The school and the loan servicer are one hand. They sold you the loan, not the future.

patterns.name: WAGE CAPTURE
patterns.lesson: Wages kept just low enough that you need the loan to live — so you work to pay the lender.

patterns.name: NO ADDRESS, NO JOB
patterns.lesson: Lose the job, lose the home; no address, no hire. The two feed each other into a spiral.

patterns.name: ZIP-CODE DESTINY
patterns.lesson: School funding tied to property values — the block the Machine drained gets the worst schools.

patterns.name: THE EXPENDABLE WORKER
patterns.lesson: Misclassified so there's no workers' comp and no benefits — get hurt and you're discarded.

patterns.name: THE PIPELINE TO NOWHERE
patterns.lesson: Trained and charged for jobs that don't exist. School-to-dead-end by design.

patterns.name: THE EXTRACTION ZONE
patterns.lesson: No jobs, predatory credit, housing that builds no wealth. Concentrated poverty, engineered.

patterns.name: THE WIPEOUT
patterns.lesson: Medical event → debt → lose the house. A whole family erased in one bad year.

patterns.name: THE SOLD FUTURE
patterns.lesson: Debt diploma + no jobs + more loans. Paying forever for a door that was never open.

patterns.name: THE CAPTURED CITY
patterns.lesson: All five in the grip — generational poverty, by design. The whole machine, out in the open.

owners.The Algorithm: Relentless. The Machine strikes one extra time every round.
owners.The Lobbyist: Each round it leans on your strongest unfinished district (+1 Squeeze). On reveal it knocks one woken district back to Clarity 1.
owners.The Debt Buyer: Every TAKE on a trap costs +1 extra Shady. Each round, collections calls: anyone carrying Shady loses 1 Trust. The Fallen strike twice as hard.
owners.The Recruiter: Each round it peels someone away: a random player loses 1 Read in a district they can read.

scenarios.The Eviction Wave: Housing starts under siege (Squeeze 2). Hold the line.
scenarios.Payday Season: Every second round is payday: Lending takes an extra hit. The hardest rung.
scenarios.The Closure: A school starts captured (3 Squeeze). Reclaim it — fast.
scenarios.The Audit: The Machine is distracted — the block gets a one-round head start.
scenarios.A Quiet Year: No extra Squeeze. Learn the ropes.
scenarios.The Plants Close: Dayton, 2008: Labor starts at Squeeze 2, and everyone starts with 1 Trust instead of 2.
scenarios.The Hospital Closes: Dayton, 2018: Health starts at Squeeze 2, and negotiating a Health deal costs 2 Trust.

LENDING.title: The Freedman's Savings Bank
LENDING.place: Washington, D.C., with branches across the South
LENDING.story: Congress chartered a bank for the formerly enslaved, and tens of thousands opened accounts. Its white trustees moved the deposits into risky loans and speculation. When it failed in 1874, many families lost savings they had worked for since freedom.
LENDING.lesson: Always ask whose hands are on your money.

LENDING.title: Maggie L. Walker's Penny Savings Bank
LENDING.story: Maggie Lena Walker chartered the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank so Black families could save, borrow and buy homes on fair terms. She was the first woman of any race to charter a bank in the United States.
LENDING.lesson: If they won't lend to you fairly, build the bank.

HOUSING.title: The Redlining Maps
HOUSING.story: The federal Home Owners' Loan Corporation graded neighborhoods for lending risk. Black neighborhoods were routinely shaded red, "hazardous," which cut them off from fair mortgages for generations.
HOUSING.lesson: The map was drawn on purpose. It can be redrawn on purpose.

HOUSING.title: The Contract Buyers League
HOUSING.story: Shut out of mortgages, Black families bought homes "on contract" at inflated prices, losing everything after one missed payment. They organized, withheld payments together and went to court, and forced many sellers to renegotiate.
HOUSING.lesson: Read the contract together. Then fight it together.

LABOR.title: I AM A MAN
LABOR.story: Black sanitation workers struck after two co-workers were killed by a faulty truck. Their signs read "I AM A MAN." Dr. King came to Memphis to stand with them. The strike won union recognition and a raise.

LABOR.title: The Montgomery Bus Boycott
LABOR.story: For 381 days, Black riders walked, carpooled and organized rather than ride segregated buses. The lost fares hurt the bus company, and the Supreme Court struck down bus segregation.
LABOR.lesson: Your money is a vote. Spend it like one.

HEALTH.title: The People's Free Medical Clinics
HEALTH.story: The Black Panther Party opened free community clinics and ran a national screening campaign for sickle cell anemia, a disease the medical system had long neglected.
HEALTH.lesson: When care won't come to the block, the block brings care.

HEALTH.title: Dr. Charles Drew
HEALTH.story: Dr. Drew pioneered ways to store blood plasma and ran a major wartime blood-bank program. He spoke out against the Red Cross separating donated blood by race.
HEALTH.lesson: Expertise is protection. Learn the system better than it knows you.

EDUCATION.title: Wilberforce University
EDUCATION.story: In 1863 the AME Church bought Wilberforce, making it the first college owned and operated by African Americans. Central State University grew up beside it. Both are minutes from Dayton.
EDUCATION.lesson: We have always built our own schools.

EDUCATION.title: Dunbar, the Wrights and the Dayton Tattler
EDUCATION.story: Paul Laurence Dunbar and Orville Wright were classmates at Dayton's Central High School. In 1890 the Wright brothers printed Dunbar's newspaper for Dayton's Black community, the Dayton Tattler.
EDUCATION.lesson: The block reads, and the block writes its own story.

ANY.title: Mayor James H. McGee
ANY.story: Dayton elected James H. McGee its first Black mayor. He served for twelve years, and a West Dayton boulevard carries his name.
ANY.lesson: Get a voice in the room where the rules are written.

ANY.title: Greenwood: Black Wall Street
ANY.story: Greenwood was a thriving Black business district of banks, theaters and shops. A white mob destroyed it in the 1921 massacre. Residents rebuilt much of it within years, with little help.
ANY.lesson: What we build can be taken. What we know can't.

BARBERSHOP.name: The Barbershop & Beauty Shop
BARBERSHOP.bonus: Your next Teach this turn is free.
BARBERSHOP.flavor: Where the news really travels. Somebody in the chair already read the fine print.

CHURCH.name: The Church
CHURCH.flavor: Come as you are. Leave a little lighter.

ADVENTURE.name: Adventure Central
ADVENTURE.bonus: Your next Study this turn gives +2 Read.
ADVENTURE.flavor: The young people's learning center in the park. Practice makes sight.

MARKET.name: Gem City Market
MARKET.where: the co-op grocery on Salem Avenue
MARKET.bonus: Your next deal this turn: draw 2, face 1.
MARKET.flavor: Owned by the neighborhood it feeds. Shop around before you sign.

KITCHEN.name: Grandma's Kitchen Table
KITCHEN.where: the house everybody ends up at
KITCHEN.bonus: Once per game: every player gets +2 Trust.
KITCHEN.flavor: Sit down. Eat. Now show me the paper they gave you.

THE_MAP.title: The Map
THE_MAP.intro: The federal maps shade the West Side red. The banks won't lend here, the insurers won't write here, and the only way to buy a house is on contract. Families start reading their contracts together.
THE_MAP.twist: REDLINING is active from round 1, and from round 2, while it stays active, the map compounds: it tightens a second time every round (+1 Squeeze on the weaker of Housing and Lending). Break it, or it breaks you.
THE_MAP.face_text: The Appraiser: leans on your strongest unfinished district every round (+1 Squeeze); on reveal, knocks one woken district back to Clarity 1.

HOUSING.front: Rent-to-Own: $25/week and the couch is yours!
HOUSING.red: Total paid = 2–4x the retail price.
HOUSING.amber: Miss one week late in the term and they take it — you keep nothing.
HOUSING.blue: The store and the lease company are one holding company.
HOUSING.basis: weekly payments adding up to two or three times the price (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Own Your Home — no bank, no mortgage! (Contract-for-Deed)
HOUSING.red: You build no equity; miss a payment late and lose it all.
HOUSING.amber: One default — even near the end — forfeits everything you paid.
HOUSING.blue: The seller reclaims and resells the same house again and again.
HOUSING.basis: years of payments on a contract house, lost with one late payment (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Just first month + deposit to move in.
HOUSING.red: Move-out charges get invented to keep your whole deposit.
HOUSING.amber: The dispute window is tight — miss it and it's gone.
HOUSING.blue: A 'turnover' vendor profits from every withheld deposit.
HOUSING.basis: a deposit kept for invented charges (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: All utilities included — simple!
HOUSING.red: A flat 'utility' charge set far above your real usage.
HOUSING.amber: The rate adjusts up yearly with no itemized proof.
HOUSING.blue: A submetering vendor splits the overcharge with ownership.
HOUSING.basis: a flat utility charge above real usage, for a year (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Standard lease, just sign here.
HOUSING.red: Waives your notice and auto-adds 'attorney fees' on any late rent.
HOUSING.amber: Late by a day → filing starts and fees attach immediately.
HOUSING.blue: A high-volume eviction law firm is paid per filing by the group.
HOUSING.basis: fees added to one late rent (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: A house on the next street, and they're finally selling to us!
HOUSING.red: Bought cheap from panicked sellers, then marked up by half or more for you.
HOUSING.amber: Sold on contract: you won't hold the deed until the very last payment.
HOUSING.blue: The same speculator scared the sellers into selling and now sells to you. That's blockbusting.
HOUSING.basis: a house marked up by half after panic selling (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Fire insurance: our special policy for your area.
HOUSING.red: It costs far more than the same policy across the line, when they'll write one at all.
HOUSING.amber: One claim and the policy is cancelled at renewal.
HOUSING.blue: Insurers drew the same red lines the lenders did.
HOUSING.basis: a year of an overpriced 'special' policy (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: A room in a converted house: cheap, and close to the plant.
HOUSING.red: Per square foot, the rent is higher than the big houses across town.
HOUSING.amber: The rent climbs as more families are packed into the building.
HOUSING.blue: An absentee owner splits big houses into many units; the more crowded, the more profit.
HOUSING.basis: a year of rent above what bigger houses cost across town (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Urban renewal: the city will buy your home. Progress is coming!
HOUSING.red: The payout is far below what it costs to buy anywhere you're allowed to live.
HOUSING.amber: Refuse, and eminent domain takes the house anyway, on their schedule.
HOUSING.blue: The highways and the 'renewal' land went where the red lines were drawn.
HOUSING.basis: a buyout below what any allowed house costs (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: A nice house across town. The realtor says you'd love it there.
HOUSING.red: The deed carries a covenant: no Black owners.
HOUSING.amber: Since Shelley v. Kraemer (1948) courts can't enforce it, but the realtor won't tell you that.
HOUSING.blue: Developers, realtors and lenders wrote those covenants in together.
HOUSING.basis: a deposit lost on a house the covenant won't let you keep (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Home repair: we'll fix your roof today. Just sign here.
HOUSING.red: The 'repair loan' is secured by your house, at a crushing rate.
HOUSING.amber: Miss payments and the lender can take the house over a roof.
HOUSING.blue: The contractor and the lender split the loan.
HOUSING.basis: a repair loan secured by the house, at a crushing rate (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: The bank's appraiser: sorry, this block appraises low.
HOUSING.red: Your home is valued below what it would fetch across the line.
HOUSING.amber: The low appraisal blocks the refinance you needed this year.
HOUSING.blue: For decades the appraisal manuals graded Black neighborhoods down by rule.
HOUSING.basis: the value a low appraisal takes off your home (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: A GI Bill home loan, and this veteran actually got one.
HOUSING.red: A guaranteed mortgage at a fair rate, with a small down payment.
HOUSING.amber: Fixed payments and a clear schedule. Many Black veterans were denied; this one wasn't.
HOUSING.blue: A public benefit, earned in service.
HOUSING.basis: a fair mortgage with a small down payment (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: File a fair-housing complaint about the realtor who steered you away.
HOUSING.red: Free to file, and steering is against the law since the Fair Housing Act (1968).
HOUSING.amber: There's a deadline, so write down names and dates now.
HOUSING.blue: The law is on your side, and so is the agency that enforces it.
HOUSING.basis: a home you're no longer steered away from (1950s dollars)

HOUSING.front: The church's building fund helps a family make a fair down payment.
HOUSING.red: No interest; the congregation pools money so you can buy with a real deed.
HOUSING.amber: Pay it back on a schedule the trustees agree with you, in the open.
HOUSING.blue: The block financing the block.
HOUSING.basis: a down payment with no interest (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Pawn: cash now for your item, buy it back anytime.
LENDING.red: Effective APR 120–240%; most items are never redeemed.
LENDING.amber: The redemption window is short — miss it and it's sold.
LENDING.blue: Resale profit flows to the same chain that wrote the loan.
LENDING.basis: high interest on a pawn, or the item gone (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Check Cashing: cash your check instantly, no bank needed.
LENDING.red: 1–5% per check — hundreds a year to reach your own money.
LENDING.amber: Every payday, every time. It never stops.
LENDING.blue: The chain also sells the payday loans you'll 'need' next.
LENDING.basis: a fee on every check, for a year (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Debt Consolidation: one low monthly payment, be debt-free!
LENDING.red: Lower payment = longer term = more interest paid in total.
LENDING.amber: Stop paying creditors as told and your credit craters first.
LENDING.blue: The 'nonprofit' is funded by fees from the lenders it deals with.
LENDING.basis: more interest over a longer term (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: The small-loan company: easy terms for working people.
LENDING.red: Around 3% a month in interest: more than a third of the loan every year.
LENDING.amber: Late fees stack on top, and the loan renews before it's paid down.
LENDING.blue: Small-loan laws set the ceiling high, and the lenders helped write them.
LENDING.basis: 3% a month on a small loan, for a year (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: The downtown bank: open a savings account with us!
LENDING.red: They'll hold your savings, but they won't lend a dollar on your street.
LENDING.amber: Your deposits fund mortgages across the line, year after year.
LENDING.blue: The red line on the federal map decides who gets to borrow.
LENDING.basis: savings that fund loans everywhere but your street (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Furniture on time: a little each week.
LENDING.red: The weekly price adds up to double the sticker or more.
LENDING.amber: Miss a week and they come for the whole set, paid-off pieces included.
LENDING.blue: The store makes more on the credit than on the furniture.
LENDING.basis: weekly furniture payments that double the price (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: A burial policy from the insurance man: just a dime a week.
LENDING.red: You pay in for years; most policies like this lapse with nothing paid out.
LENDING.amber: Miss a few weeks and the policy lapses. Everything you paid stays with them.
LENDING.blue: Lapsed policies are the company's profit.
LENDING.basis: years of dimes on a policy that lapses (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Borrow against your next paychecks: sign the wage assignment.
LENDING.red: The lender takes your pay straight from your employer.
LENDING.amber: One late payment and your boss gets the notice, and may let you go.
LENDING.blue: Lenders and employers both profit from the hold it gives them over workers.
LENDING.basis: pay taken straight from your employer (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Easy credit at the clothing store: no money down!
LENDING.red: Prices are marked up for credit customers, then interest goes on top.
LENDING.amber: The balance never seems to shrink before the next purchase.
LENDING.blue: The store sells the debt to a collector.
LENDING.basis: credit markups plus interest (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Refinance your contract: a lower payment now!
LENDING.red: Lower payment, longer term: more interest, and the balloon is still at the end.
LENDING.amber: Signing resets the clock on everything you've paid in.
LENDING.blue: The seller gets paid again, and you still don't hold the deed.
LENDING.basis: more interest, and the balloon still at the end (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Sell your next paycheck at a discount: cash today.
LENDING.red: You hand over a full week's pay for most of it now. The discount is the interest.
LENDING.amber: Every payday it's due again, and it never stops.
LENDING.blue: Salary buyers worked the plant gates every payday.
LENDING.basis: a week's pay sold at a discount (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: Co-sign for your cousin's car. It's family.
LENDING.red: You owe every dollar if they can't pay.
LENDING.amber: Their missed payment shows up on your name the same month.
LENDING.blue: Lenders count on family ties to collect.
LENDING.basis: every dollar of a car loan you cosigned (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: A Black-owned savings and loan: a fair mortgage, on your street.
LENDING.red: A fair rate. They lend where the downtown banks won't.
LENDING.amber: Clear terms, and you hold the deed from day one.
LENDING.blue: Owned by the community it lends to.
LENDING.basis: a fair mortgage on your own street (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: The credit union at the plant: a small loan at a fair rate.
LENDING.red: A capped rate, and members vote on how it's run.
LENDING.amber: Payments come out of pay you agreed to, and stop when it's paid.
LENDING.blue: Member-owned: the profit comes back to the workers.
LENDING.basis: a small loan at a capped rate (1950s dollars)

LENDING.front: The mutual-aid society: a loan from the club when you need it.
LENDING.red: No interest: the members pooled it for exactly this.
LENDING.amber: Pay it back as you can; the club knows your name.
LENDING.blue: Neighbors covering neighbors, the way the block always has.
LENDING.basis: a loan from the club, with no interest (1950s dollars)

league.name: The League
league.text: Like the Contract Buyers League (Chicago, 1968): sign the pledge to withhold together (an action). Every family must sign in the same round, or the sellers scare them off and the pledges fall apart. Once it forms: Housing Squeeze −2 at once, Housing −1 every second round after, and every Housing and Lending trap can be negotiated with Read 1.

decision.text: Stay and fight for the house, or move to where the map says you can?

options.label: Stay and fight
options.text: Housing keeps its stickers, and the family's Ledger +1: they held the line.

options.label: Move
options.text: Remove one Scar from Housing, but the Elder stays behind: in Chapter 4 the Elder starts with no Read and no History.

FREEDOMS_LEDGER.title: Freedom's Ledger
FREEDOMS_LEDGER.intro: The family is newly free. They save what they can, learn to read by lamplight, raise a church and a school, and sign the only contracts on offer: the crop lien, the store's book, the year-long labor contract.
FREEDOMS_LEDGER.twist: Nobody starts with Read, not even the Elder: the family learns everything at the table. And the crop lien grips from the first day: Lending starts at Squeeze 2.
FREEDOMS_LEDGER.face_text: The Planter's Ledger: every shortcut costs +1 extra Shady, and each round the store calls in its book: anyone carrying Shady loses 1 Trust. The Fallen strike twice as hard.

LENDING.front: Take what you need from the store, and we'll settle up at harvest.
LENDING.red: Everything on credit is priced well above what cash customers pay for the same goods.
LENDING.amber: The bill comes due at settlement, out of your crop, before you see a dollar.
LENDING.blue: The store keeps the only copy of the account.
LENDING.basis: a year of meal, meat and cloth at credit prices above cash (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: No money down: we'll carry you on the books all year.
LENDING.red: Interest goes on the account too, on top of the credit prices.
LENDING.amber: It is figured at settlement, when it's too late to shop anywhere else.
LENDING.blue: You can't check the books, and he knows it.
LENDING.basis: interest charged on a year's store account (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: Sign the crop lien and the merchant will furnish you till harvest.
LENDING.red: The lien gives him first claim on your whole crop, not just what you owe.
LENDING.amber: Sign before planting or go without. At harvest the cotton goes to him first.
LENDING.blue: Lien laws passed after the war put the merchant ahead of the family that grew it.
LENDING.basis: a crop pledged against a year of furnish (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: Short this year? Don't worry, we'll carry the balance to next season.
LENDING.red: The balance keeps its interest, and next year's goods go on top of it.
LENDING.amber: The carried debt binds you to the same store and the same land next year.
LENDING.blue: A family that owes can't leave, and he needs hands.
LENDING.basis: a balance carried over with interest into the next year (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: Fertilizer on credit: buy it now, pay at harvest.
LENDING.red: The credit price is far higher than the cash price in town.
LENDING.amber: It goes on the same lien as the rest, due at settlement.
LENDING.blue: The merchant buys it for cash and sells it to you on time.
LENDING.basis: a season of fertilizer at the credit price (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: Bring your cotton here. We'll weigh it and price it for you.
LENDING.red: His scale and his grading pay you less than the cotton would bring in town.
LENDING.amber: Your share is settled on his numbers the same day.
LENDING.blue: The man who weighs your cotton is the man you owe.
LENDING.basis: cotton weighed light and graded low at one settlement (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: A little cash for Christmas, against your share.
LENDING.red: The advance is charged back to your share with interest added.
LENDING.amber: It comes out at next settlement, before anything else.
LENDING.blue: Small advances keep the account from ever coming out even.
LENDING.basis: a holiday advance repaid with interest (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: Put up your mule and your plow, just as security.
LENDING.red: The mortgage covers the tools you need to farm at all.
LENDING.amber: One short year and he can take the mule and the plow.
LENDING.blue: Without a mule, the family has to farm on his terms.
LENDING.basis: a mule and tools held under a chattel mortgage (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: Buy this land from me on time, and pay it off in cotton.
LENDING.red: The price is high, and the payments come out of crops he also sells you credit against.
LENDING.amber: Miss one year's payment and the land goes back, with everything you paid.
LENDING.blue: He keeps the deed until the very last bale.
LENDING.basis: years of land payments lost with one missed year (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: The planter's store is the only one for miles, and he'll handle your account.
LENDING.red: The rent, the store bill and your share are all on one man's books.
LENDING.amber: Settlement day is his to choose, and so is the final figure.
LENDING.blue: The landlord and the merchant are the same man, so every side of the ledger is his.
LENDING.basis: a year's share settled on one man's books (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: A deed to forty acres, cheap. Pay me now before the land is gone.
LENDING.red: The paper costs you your savings, and the land it names isn't for sale.
LENDING.amber: The seller is gone before anyone checks the title.
LENDING.blue: The land promised in 1865 went back to the old owners, and swindlers sold the hope.
LENDING.basis: savings paid for a land title that was worthless (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: The Freedman's Savings Bank: a safe place for your savings.
LENDING.red: A passbook, interest on what you save, and you can deposit as little as you have.
LENDING.amber: Take your money out at the branch when you need it. Congress chartered it in 1865.
LENDING.blue: White trustees made risky loans with deposits; it failed in 1874, and savers lost most of what they had.
LENDING.basis: a family's savings in a passbook (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: The benevolent society: dues each month, and help when sickness or a burial comes.
LENDING.red: Small dues, set by the members in meeting, written down for all to see.
LENDING.amber: Pay on the meeting day; the help comes when you need it, not at harvest.
LENDING.blue: Members chose their own officers, often through the church, and covered each other.
LENDING.basis: a year of sick and burial help from the society (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: Families pool their savings to buy land together, with a real deed.
LENDING.red: Each family puts in what it can, and the price is the seller's cash price.
LENDING.amber: The deed is recorded at the courthouse, with each family's share written down.
LENDING.blue: Neighbors owning the ground they work, the way many freed families did.
LENDING.basis: a family's share of land bought together (1870s dollars)

LENDING.front: Pay cash from the egg and garden money, at the cash price.
LENDING.red: No credit price, no interest, and no lien on the crop.
LENDING.amber: Nothing is due at settlement for what you already paid for.
LENDING.blue: Money the family made itself, kept off the merchant's books.
LENDING.basis: credit markups avoided on a season of goods (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Work my land on shares: you keep half of everything you raise.
LABOR.red: Your half comes after the furnish, the fines and the store bill are taken out.
LABOR.amber: Nothing is paid until the crop is in and sold.
LABOR.blue: The landlord keeps the books on both halves.
LABOR.basis: a family's half share after charges (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Paid in store orders, good at the plantation store.
LABOR.red: Orders buy less there than the same pay would buy in cash in town.
LABOR.amber: They're only good at one store, so you shop there all year.
LABOR.blue: The planter profits on the wages and again on the store.
LABOR.basis: a year of wages spent at one store's prices (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Lost time is just docked from your share. That's only fair.
LABOR.red: Fines for sick days, rain days and talking back come off your pay.
LABOR.amber: The fines are tallied at settlement, when you can't dispute them.
LABOR.blue: Contracts let the employer set the fines and keep the count.
LABOR.basis: fines and docked days over a season (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Pick for me at harvest, paid by the pound, weighed on my scale.
LABOR.red: A light scale pays you for less cotton than you picked.
LABOR.amber: You're paid at the end of picking, on his tally.
LABOR.blue: The man who owns the scale decides what you picked.
LABOR.basis: a picking season weighed light (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Just make your mark here. I'll keep the accounts for you.
LABOR.red: His figures say you owe more than your share is worth.
LABOR.amber: The contract you marked runs a full year.
LABOR.blue: Signing what you can't read leaves every number to him.
LABOR.basis: a year's share settled on figures you can't check (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Sign for the year, and you'll be paid in full at the end of the season.
LABOR.red: Your wages are held all year and paid in one lump, if at all.
LABOR.amber: Leave before the season ends and you can lose the whole year's pay.
LABOR.blue: Holding the pay till harvest kept workers from leaving.
LABOR.basis: a year of farm wages held until settlement (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Sign a contract by January, or the law calls you a vagrant.
LABOR.red: You sign with whoever is in front of you, on whatever terms, to avoid a fine.
LABOR.amber: The 1865 codes set a January deadline, but by 1867 federal law had set most of them aside.
LABOR.blue: Planter legislatures wrote the codes to force freed people back to the fields.
LABOR.basis: a year bound to a contract signed under threat (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Let us take the children as apprentices: fed, clothed and taught a trade.
LABOR.red: The children work for no pay, often for their former owner.
LABOR.amber: They're bound until they come of age, and leaving means being brought back.
LABOR.blue: The codes let courts bind Black children away from parents who wanted them home.
LABOR.basis: a child's unpaid labor for a year (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Stay through the settlement and we'll square up when the cotton's sold.
LABOR.red: The cotton sells, but the settlement keeps getting put off.
LABOR.amber: By the time he settles, next year's contract is already due.
LABOR.blue: Late settlement keeps the family on the place another year.
LABOR.basis: a share held back past the end of the year (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Stay on with me. Nobody else around here will hire you anyway.
LABOR.red: You take lower terms because there seems to be no choice.
LABOR.amber: Leave under contract and you can be brought back.
LABOR.blue: Enticement laws fined any planter who hired a worker away, so they kept wages down together.
LABOR.basis: lower terms with no one allowed to bid for your work (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Can't pay the vagrancy fine? I'll pay it, and you work it off for me.
LABOR.red: You work for him until he says the fine and costs are paid.
LABOR.amber: There's no set end, and his figures decide when you're free to go.
LABOR.blue: Under the codes, sheriffs could hire out people who couldn't pay; the law and the planter worked as one.
LABOR.basis: unpaid work to pay off a fine and court costs (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: Good wages out west. The agent pays your passage; the train leaves tomorrow.
LABOR.red: The fare is a debt, taken back out of wages that are lower than he said.
LABOR.amber: Leave tomorrow, sign there, and you're bound to a planter you've never met.
LABOR.blue: Labor agents were paid by the head by planters short of hands.
LABOR.basis: fare and fees taken out of a year's wages (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: The teacher at the freedmen's school will read the contract with you first.
LABOR.red: No charge. Every term is read aloud before anyone makes a mark.
LABOR.amber: Take a day to think it over; a fair offer will still be there.
LABOR.blue: Freed people built and filled these schools themselves, with churches and northern teachers.
LABOR.basis: a contract you understood before you signed (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: A contract written out fairly and witnessed, with pay set down in plain numbers.
LABOR.red: Wages or shares written in full, with no fines left blank.
LABOR.amber: Paydays are in writing, and a witness holds a copy.
LABOR.blue: A witness, often a Freedmen's Bureau agent, meant the terms could be held to.
LABOR.basis: a year of pay on terms someone else can check (1870s dollars)

LABOR.front: The neighbors agree together on what terms they'll take this year.
LABOR.red: No one undercuts anyone, so the whole place bargains as one.
LABOR.amber: Decide before contract time, and hold to it together.
LABOR.blue: Freed families often bargained as groups, and planters short of hands had to listen.
LABOR.basis: better terms bargained for together (1870s dollars)

decision.text: Go north now, or stay one more season and save?

options.label: Go north now
options.text: Chapter 2 starts with all five districts open from round 1.

options.label: Stay and save
options.text: The family's Ledger +1, but Chapter 2 starts with Lending at Squeeze 1 (the debt follows you).

UP_NORTH.title: Up North
UP_NORTH.intro: The family steps off the train on Dayton's West Side with a labor agent's ticket and a room they haven't seen. The plants are hiring. The fine print came north too.
UP_NORTH.twist: Only Lending, Housing and Labor are open at first. Health and Education open in round 3, once the family is settled.
UP_NORTH.face_text: The Labor Agent: every round it leans on your strongest unfinished district (+1 Squeeze); on reveal, knocks one woken district back to Clarity 1.

LABOR.front: Good jobs up north, and I'll get you the ticket, paid back out of your wages.
LABOR.red: The fare comes out of your pay with his fee on top, at whatever price he names.
LABOR.amber: Until it's paid off, he or the company holds your first pay envelopes.
LABOR.blue: The agent gets paid by you and by the company for every worker he delivers.
LABOR.basis: a train fare north plus the agent's fee, taken from wages (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: Two dollars to the employment office and you start Monday, but the line's long, so pay now.
LABOR.red: The fee is gone whether the job lasts a month, a week or not at all.
LABOR.amber: Jobs like this often end in days, and the next placement costs another fee.
LABOR.blue: Some offices split their fees with foremen, who had reason to fire and rehire.
LABOR.basis: placement fees paid over and over for short jobs (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: The foundry pays every week, and it's steady work for a strong man.
LABOR.red: It's the hottest, most dangerous job on the floor, at a lower rate than the jobs inside.
LABOR.amber: Burns and bad lungs add up, and a hurt man is the first one let go.
LABOR.blue: The plant fills its worst jobs with Black workers and keeps the better ones closed to them.
LABOR.basis: lower pay for the hottest job, over a year (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: We dock a little for breakage, that's all, everybody pays it.
LABOR.red: Broken tools and spoiled work come out of your pay, and the foreman decides how much.
LABOR.amber: The docking comes every payday, and nobody shows you the count.
LABOR.blue: Nobody checks the foreman's numbers, and fines cost the plant less than fixing machines.
LABOR.basis: pay docked for 'breakage' over a year (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: Be at the gate by six for the shape-up, and the boss picks who works today.
LABOR.red: You wait unpaid for hours, and some bosses want a cut to pick you again.
LABOR.amber: No pick, no pay, and no telling if you'll work tomorrow either.
LABOR.blue: A crowd at the gate every morning keeps the day rate low for everyone.
LABOR.basis: days lost waiting at the gate, over a year (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: You're hired, welcome aboard, the plant is growing fast.
LABOR.red: You start at the bottom rate, with no seniority and no say over your job.
LABOR.amber: When orders drop you're the first laid off, and the last called back.
LABOR.blue: Hiring and layoff rules kept Black workers at the bottom of every list.
LABOR.basis: months laid off in a slow year (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: Between paydays we pay in store orders, good as cash at the company store.
LABOR.red: Store prices run high, and the orders are only good there.
LABOR.amber: By the time payday comes, the store has already taken most of it.
LABOR.blue: The company owns the store and makes money on both ends of your pay.
LABOR.basis: a year of marked-up prices at the company store (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: Work the whole season and we pay you everything in one lump at the end.
LABOR.red: Part of every week's wages is held back, and you live on what's left.
LABOR.amber: Quit early, or get let go a week short, and the held pay is forfeit.
LABOR.blue: The held-back wages are a free loan to the company, and some never get paid.
LABOR.basis: a season's held-back wages lost by leaving early (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: Piece rate: the faster you work, the more you take home!
LABOR.red: You work yourself ragged to earn what the hourly men get.
LABOR.amber: Once enough men hit the number, the rate is cut and the fast pace becomes the floor.
LABOR.blue: Time-study men set the rates to get more work for the same pay.
LABOR.basis: rate cuts after the pace goes up, over a year (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: Steady job, top pay, start right now, no questions asked.
LABOR.red: You'll cross a picket line, and the men on it will remember your face.
LABOR.amber: The day the strike settles, you're let go, and the job was never yours.
LABOR.blue: The company hired you to break a strike, and nobody told you.
LABOR.basis: pay lost when a strikebreaker job ends with the strike (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: Join the company club: picnics, a ball team and a little insurance.
LABOR.red: It looks free, but it's meant to cost you a voice at work.
LABOR.amber: The insurance and the bonus only pay if you stay, and stay quiet.
LABOR.blue: The company runs the club to keep workers out of the union.
LABOR.basis: a year of benefits that vanish if you speak up (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: Just sign this promise that you won't join a union, then you start.
LABOR.red: You give up the right to join a union in exchange for the job.
LABOR.amber: Join anyway and you can be fired on the spot, and the courts backed the boss.
LABOR.blue: Employers wrote these 'yellow-dog' contracts so workers couldn't bargain together.
LABOR.basis: raises a union might have won, over a year (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: The colored branch of the Y keeps a job board and a list of clean rooms for newcomers.
LABOR.red: Free to look, with a small membership fee if you stay on.
LABOR.amber: No contract and no fee owed to the job it sends you to.
LABOR.blue: Run by Black Dayton, for the people stepping off the train.
LABOR.basis: agent and placement fees you don't have to pay (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: A union card from the CIO: they're organizing the whole plant, Black and white together.
LABOR.red: Dues of about a dollar a month, and the contract wins it back in raises.
LABOR.amber: Seniority is written down, and the same rules hold for every member.
LABOR.blue: Members vote, and the union's strength is that nobody gets left out.
LABOR.basis: a year of raises and protected seniority (1920s dollars)

LABOR.front: The men's club at church passes the word on who's hiring and which agents to avoid.
LABOR.red: Free: you just pass the word on to the next family that comes up.
LABOR.amber: The news is fresh every Sunday, so ask before you sign anything.
LABOR.blue: Neighbors who already learned the hard way, looking out for you.
LABOR.basis: a bad agent's fee and a lost week avoided (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: A room in my boarding house, meals included, and you pay by the week.
HOUSING.red: A shared room by the week costs more than a whole flat across town.
HOUSING.amber: Miss one week and your trunk stays locked in the room until you pay.
HOUSING.blue: Newcomers have few places to go, and the boarding-house keeper knows it.
HOUSING.basis: a year of weekly board for a shared room (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: A kitchenette of your own, cut out of the big house on the corner.
HOUSING.red: One room, a hot plate and a bathroom down the hall, at a whole flat's rent.
HOUSING.amber: The rent climbs as more families get packed into the house.
HOUSING.blue: The owner makes more by cutting one house into many rooms.
HOUSING.basis: a year of rent above what the space is worth (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: The rent is what it is, and you won't find better on this side.
HOUSING.red: Black tenants pay more than white tenants pay for the same rooms, or better ones.
HOUSING.amber: Every year more families arrive, and the rent goes up again.
HOUSING.blue: The lines keep you on this side, so the landlord can charge what he likes.
HOUSING.basis: a year of rent marked up above what white tenants paid (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Rent's high, sure, but take in a lodger or two and it covers itself.
HOUSING.red: Your family gives up a room and its privacy so the rent can be paid.
HOUSING.amber: When the landlord sees the lodgers, the rent goes up to match.
HOUSING.blue: The rent was set high counting on families crowding in to pay it.
HOUSING.basis: a room's rent passed along to lodgers, over a year (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Furnish the whole flat for a dollar down, but the sale ends Saturday.
HOUSING.red: The weekly payments add up to twice the sticker price or more.
HOUSING.amber: Miss one week and they come for all of it, even the pieces you've paid off.
HOUSING.blue: The store makes more on the credit than on the furniture.
HOUSING.basis: weekly payments that double the price of a houseful of furniture (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: No lease needed, you can move in today and pay week to week.
HOUSING.red: No lease means no promise about repairs, heat or anything else.
HOUSING.amber: The rent can go up any week, and you can be put out on short notice.
HOUSING.blue: Week-to-week tenants are easy to squeeze and easy to replace.
HOUSING.basis: a year of rent raises with no lease to stop them (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Pay the key money today and the flat is yours; three families are waiting behind you.
HOUSING.red: A cash payment just to get the key, on top of the rent.
HOUSING.amber: Move out, or get put out, and the key money is gone.
HOUSING.blue: The agent pockets it, and the shortage behind it was made by the lines.
HOUSING.basis: key money paid just to get in the door (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: I'll fix the roof and the stove next month, so just sign for the year.
HOUSING.red: You pay full rent on a place that's falling apart around you.
HOUSING.amber: Next month never comes, and you're bound to the place for the year.
HOUSING.blue: The owner lives across town, and every repair comes out of his profit.
HOUSING.basis: a year of rent on repairs that never happen (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: Heat is included all winter long, so you never have to buy a lump of coal!
HOUSING.red: The furnace runs a few hours a day, so you buy your own coal to stay warm.
HOUSING.amber: Complain and your lease isn't renewed in the spring.
HOUSING.blue: The owner saves on coal, and you pay for it twice.
HOUSING.basis: a winter of your own coal on top of 'heat included' (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: A nice house across the river, and the owner says the price is right.
HOUSING.red: The deed carries a covenant that bars Black owners from the house.
HOUSING.amber: The neighbors can sue to undo the sale, and in these years the courts enforced it.
HOUSING.blue: Developers and neighborhood associations wrote those covenants in to hold the line.
HOUSING.basis: a deposit lost on a house the covenant won't let you keep (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: The real estate man says the West Side is where you'd be happiest.
HOUSING.red: Your choices shrink to the oldest, most crowded blocks in the city.
HOUSING.amber: Every year more families are pushed into the same streets, and rents climb.
HOUSING.blue: The realtors' own code of ethics told agents to keep Black families out of white blocks.
HOUSING.basis: a year of higher rent in a crowded, confined market (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: The rent collector's a friendly fellow from the neighborhood, and he'll work with you.
HOUSING.red: Same high rent, same broken stairs: the friendly face doesn't set the price.
HOUSING.amber: When you fall behind, the notice comes from the owner's lawyer, not from him.
HOUSING.blue: The owner lives across town and never sets foot in the building.
HOUSING.basis: a year of rent and late charges to an absentee owner (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: The lodge's sick-and-burial fund helps a member's family make rent in a bad month.
HOUSING.red: Monthly dues, and the benefit is paid when you're sick or grieving.
HOUSING.amber: No interest, no papers to trap you, just the lodge's rules read out loud.
HOUSING.blue: Owned by the members, who are your neighbors.
HOUSING.basis: a month or two of rent covered in a crisis (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: A building and loan run by our own people: save a little each week toward a house.
HOUSING.red: Weekly payments buy shares, and a fair loan comes when you've saved enough.
HOUSING.amber: A clear schedule, and the deed is in your name.
HOUSING.blue: The members are the owners, and the money stays on the block.
HOUSING.basis: a fair home loan from savings pooled by members (1920s dollars)

HOUSING.front: The church keeps a list of decent rooms and fair landlords for families just off the train.
HOUSING.red: Free: the church asks only that you come by on Sunday.
HOUSING.amber: No lease trick and no rush; they'll tell you which landlords to avoid.
HOUSING.blue: The congregation looking after the people who just arrived.
HOUSING.basis: overpriced rent and a lost deposit avoided (1920s dollars)

unlocks_always: Dunbar, the Wrights and the Dayton Tattler
unlocks_if_won: Maggie L. Walker's Penny Savings Bank

decision.text: The family has a little saved. Put it into the church, the house, or a child's schooling?

options.label: The church
options.text: In Chapter 3, gathering at the church takes off 3 Shady instead of 2.

options.label: The house
options.text: In Chapter 3, Housing starts with 1 less Squeeze: a house the family owns outright.

options.label: A child's schooling
options.text: In Chapter 3, the Student starts with Read 1 everywhere.

VOICE.title: Voice
VOICE.intro: Boycotts in Montgomery, a strike in Memphis, and on the West Side the family is registering voters. In 1970 Dayton elects James H. McGee mayor. Somebody keeps offering the organizers a quieter way.
VOICE.twist: The Organizer's NEGOTIATE clears 3 Squeeze. Once per game, any player can call the March (an action): every player gathers at once (Trust +2, Shady −1, covered).
VOICE.face_text: The Council: leans on your strongest unfinished district every round (+1 Squeeze); on reveal, it redraws the lines: every woken district loses 1 Clarity.

LABOR.front: Plenty of steady work at the foundry for you, out in the hot end.
LABOR.red: The hot, dirty jobs pay the least, and the better-paid departments won't take you.
LABOR.amber: You can work there twenty years and still be in the same job at the same rate.
LABOR.blue: The plant's job ladder was drawn by race: some rungs were never open to you.
LABOR.basis: a year of the pay gap between the hot end and the better departments (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: The city sanitation crew is hiring: steady pay, start tomorrow.
LABOR.red: The pay is so low that some full-time crews still can't feed their families.
LABOR.amber: Send the crew home for rain and there's no pay for the day.
LABOR.blue: With no union to answer to, the city sets the pay and the conditions alone.
LABOR.basis: a year of pay below what a family needs (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: Day work at the gate: cash in your hand at the end of every shift.
LABOR.red: The labor contractor takes his cut out of every day's pay before you see it.
LABOR.amber: There's no promise of tomorrow; you're back at the gate at dawn to try again.
LABOR.blue: The plant pays the contractor, so nobody on the books ever owes you anything.
LABOR.basis: the contractor's cut of a year of day pay (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: A good family across town needs help in the house, five days a week.
LABOR.red: No minimum wage and no overtime: the federal wage law left household workers out.
LABOR.amber: Long days, and you can be let go the same afternoon with no notice.
LABOR.blue: The law that protected the plant floor was written to leave this work out.
LABOR.basis: a year of household pay with no minimum wage or overtime (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: The employment agency will place you this week; the fee comes out of your first checks.
LABOR.red: The fee eats weeks of pay, and it's owed even if the job ends early.
LABOR.amber: Lose the job in the first month and you can owe the agency more than you earned.
LABOR.blue: The agency and the employer both get paid from your wages.
LABOR.basis: an agency fee taken from the first weeks of pay (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: You're hired, temporary for now; permanent comes later.
LABOR.red: Same work, same pay as the man beside you, for now.
LABOR.amber: Temporary workers build no seniority and can be let go any day, no reason given.
LABOR.blue: March on a workday or sign a union card, and 'temporary' is how they let you go.
LABOR.basis: a year of wages lost when temporary workers are let go first (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: Move up to the better department: higher pay, and it's yours on Monday.
LABOR.red: It's a real raise, and the work is cleaner.
LABOR.amber: The transfer wipes out your years of seniority, so you're the first laid off.
LABOR.blue: Separate seniority lists by department kept Black workers in the worst jobs.
LABOR.basis: a year of pay lost to being laid off first (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: Apprenticeship applications are open this week; bring a letter from a member.
LABOR.red: Applying is free, and a skilled trade pays far more than labor.
LABOR.amber: The window opens and closes in days, and it's posted only inside the hall.
LABOR.blue: The sponsor must be a member, and the members sponsor their own sons and nephews.
LABOR.basis: a year of the higher pay of a skilled trade (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: Register to vote at the board of elections, weekdays during business hours.
LABOR.red: There's no fee, but you lose a day's pay to stand in that line.
LABOR.amber: Registration closes weeks before the election; miss it and wait for the next one.
LABOR.blue: Hours set for people who can leave work are hours set to keep others out.
LABOR.basis: a day's pay lost to register (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: The company wants you as its first Black foreman. Congratulations.
LABOR.red: It's a real raise and a real title, with your name on the door.
LABOR.amber: You start next week, paid every Friday, and they need your answer by tomorrow.
LABOR.blue: It's offered to the man leading the strike committee, the week before the vote.
LABOR.basis: a foreman's raise, for a year (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: The union hall has a staff job for you: good salary, and it's indoors.
LABOR.red: Full salary and benefits, paid by the union, not the company.
LABOR.amber: It starts at once, and you'll be on the road for the international most weeks.
LABOR.blue: It takes the caucus leader off the plant floor before the fight over seniority.
LABOR.basis: a year's salary on staff (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: A city cleaning contract for your small business, steady work all year.
LABOR.red: Fair pay per building, paid on time every month.
LABOR.amber: A one-year contract, renewed each year if the city is satisfied.
LABOR.blue: It arrives the week you planned to lead the picket, and 'satisfied' means quiet.
LABOR.basis: a year of a city contract (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: The union local is fighting for one seniority list for the whole plant.
LABOR.red: Dues are a few dollars a month, and the contract they bargain pays far more.
LABOR.amber: Grievances have deadlines, and the steward helps you file on time.
LABOR.blue: The members vote on the contract and elect their stewards in the open.
LABOR.basis: a year of pay protected by plant-wide seniority (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: File a complaint: under the Civil Rights Act of 1964, hiring by race is illegal.
LABOR.red: It's free to file with the federal or the Ohio civil rights commission.
LABOR.amber: There's a short deadline to file, so write down names and dates now.
LABOR.blue: The law is on your side, and so are the lawyers who helped win it.
LABOR.basis: back pay a complaint can win (1960s dollars)

LABOR.front: The strike fund: the churches and the union feed families while the line holds.
LABOR.red: No cost: groceries, rent help and coal, given by neighbors and members.
LABOR.amber: It lasts as long as the strike does, and people keep giving.
LABOR.blue: The block and the union hall standing behind the people on the line.
LABOR.basis: groceries and rent help through a strike (1960s dollars)

EDUCATION.front: Your school's on double sessions: half days, but the same diploma.
EDUCATION.red: Your child gets half the hours of class the schools across town give.
EDUCATION.amber: The overcrowding grows every year, and so does the time lost.
EDUCATION.blue: New schools went up across town while this one was packed past capacity.
EDUCATION.basis: a year of class time lost to half days (1960s dollars)

EDUCATION.front: Lab fees, band fees and the class trip: all optional, of course.
EDUCATION.red: The 'optional' fees add up, and kids who can't pay sit out.
EDUCATION.amber: Each fee is due on its own date, and every child knows who didn't pay.
EDUCATION.blue: A school that runs on fees makes families pay for what the district won't fund.
